newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Patten slams curbs on HK freedoms before U.K. trip.
newsitem.headline: Patten slams curbs on HK freedoms before U.K. trip.

text.p: Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten on Friday questioned the need to curb civil liberties after China takes back the colony, as he prepared to fly to London to brief the new Labour government on "difficult" handover issues.

"What still hasn't been addressed is the question of why these changes (to civil liberties laws) are necessary in the first place," Patten told reporters on the grounds of his Government House residence.

"I've been Governor in Hong Kong for five happy years and I've never felt there was any demonstration taking place in Hong Kong -- and there have been a lot while I've been here -- which threatened the national security of China or the national security of the United Kingdom," he said.

On Thursday, Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa announced a partial retreat from his plan to amend laws on political funding and public demonstrations after Britain hands back the territory on July 1.
The new versions narrow a ban on foreign political funding and moderate planned limits on the right to protest.
They will be processed by a Beijing-backed provisional legislature preparing to take over from Hong Kong's elected Legislative Council at the handover.

Patten leaves on Saturday for the week-long trip, his last official visit to London before his role as Hong Kong's 28th and last British governor ends at the stroke of midnight on June 30 and he sails off in the royal yacht Britannia.
His agenda includes meetings with senior members of the new Labour government, including Prime Minister Tony Blair, Foreign Secretary Robin Cook and Foreign Office officials.
Patten said he would brief ministers about the situation in Hong Kong in the last weeks of the transition and discuss arrangements for the handover.

"Some quite difficult but not major issues" remain, including the "precise identity" of the people from the British and Chinese sides who will attend the gala handover ceremony on the evening of June 30, he said.
Patten put the problems down to protocol and the complexity of the arrangements.
Britain's new administration was familiar with the situation in Hong Kong and emphasised a "continuity of policy", he said.
"They're completely up to speed on all the issues," he said.

"The British government's policy on the provisional legislature is the same today as it was three months ago. We think that the establishment of the provisional legislature is wholly unjustified -- that it's damaging to Hong Kong and its reputation."

Patten also said he will meet former prime minister and current opposition leader John Major, but said he had no plans to discuss resuming any position alongside his former colleagues in the Conservative Party.
Patten is a former party chairman and is credited with engineering the Tories' unexpected win at the polls in 1992.

Before he leaves for London, Patten will be guest of honour at a party on Friday night hosted by the Democratic Party, which holds the largest number of seats in the current legislature but none in the post-handover provisional council.
